strengths: Novel technical contribution: Gumbel-Sinkhorn relaxation of sorting enables end-to-end differentiable optimization of Deletion/Insertion metrics; key insight that these metrics depend only on ordinal ranks is elegant.
Principled metric-driven approach: Directly optimizes recognized evaluation metrics rather than heuristic surrogates; more philosophically aligned with desired attribution properties.
Unified attribution framework: Meaningfully synthesizes perturbation-based (causal grounding), propagation-based (model consistency), and learning-based (efficiency) approaches.

Dense pixel-level attribution for ViTs: Produces sharp, boundary-aligned explanations at full resolution without patch-level artifacts or upsampling—clear practical advantage shown in qualitative comparisons.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Large-scale (50K ImageNet validation), multiple architectures (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt Small), 8+ metrics, ~10 baselines, multiple reference modes; strong quantitative improvements especially on Deletion and Faithfulness.
Computational efficiency: T=0 comparable to Grad-CAM (~0.016s); T=3 refinement (~0.547s) substantially faster than MDA (~13.6s) while achieving superior faithfulness.
Flexible compute-quality tradeoff: Optional test-time refinement with clear monotonic improvement enables practitioners to balance throughput and explanation fidelity.
Thoughtful training design: Grid augmentation, region-based permutation, perturbation step sampling, and regularization mitigate overfitting and spurious artifacts.
Clear presentation: Well-motivated, accessible methodology with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 2, 4, 6) and substantial appendix with detailed results.
Reproducibility: Implementation details provided (§4.1, Appendix A.1), code availability promised, sufficient detail for reimplementation.
weaknesses: Inherited metric limitations: Deletion/Insertion metrics have known shortcomings (reference image sensitivity, perturbation strategy dependence); substantial variance across reference modes in Tables 5–7 suggests instability. Crucial unaddressed question: why optimize imperfect proxy metrics, and does improvement on them guarantee better attributions?

Per-model retraining requirement: Each target model needs separate training; amortization overhead significant for interpretability pipelines that already expensive. Practical deployment cost and breakeven analysis vs. per-sample methods missing; applicability to proprietary models underdiscussed despite mention of test-time refinement.

Insufficient hyperparameter justification: Many choices manually tuned (λ_del=λ_ins=1, λ_reg=2.5×10⁻³, G∈[7,28], S=16, 30 Sinkhorn iterations) without ablation studies. Missing ablations on grid augmentation contribution, regularization impact, Sinkhorn iterations, and convergence analysis for one-epoch training; reproducibility risk if hyperparameters are brittle.

Limited theoretical analysis: No formal justification for why end-to-end soft-metric training produces superior pixel-level attributions; missing convergence guarantees and approximation error bounds between soft and hard metrics. Unclear why ranking metrics should translate to precise spatial localization.

Soft-hard metric gap under-analyzed: Gumbel-Sinkhorn soft masks approximate hard binary masks, but quantitative impact on metric quality not provided. Empirical analysis of del_AUC^soft vs. del_AUC tracking during training missing; potential systematic biases from relaxation not explored.

Incomplete MDA comparison: Direct competitor MDA performs per-sample optimization (different paradigm); speed comparison somewhat unfair (13.6s/image vs. 0.016s). Missing: quality comparison per unit compute (e.g., MDA with equivalent budget via parallelization).

Limited failure mode analysis: Few systematic failure cases documented; unclear which object categories, image types, or misclassified samples produce poor attributions. Single misclassified example (Figure 1) insufficient for understanding robustness.

Grid-based perturbation precision tradeoff: Region-level aggregation sacrifices spatial precision; grid augmentation mitigates but doesn't eliminate this. Quantitative analysis of precision loss and compute-accuracy tradeoff missing.

Scope limitations: Evaluation restricted to ImageNet classification; generalization to medical imaging, semantic/instance segmentation, or other domains untested. Architecture evaluation limited (frozen DINOv3 backbone may not generalize to radically different designs). Unclear if method benefits CNN-based models as much as ViTs.

Missing statistical significance testing: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests across 50K images. Example differences (e.g., Deletion 0.1381 vs. 0.1420) may be statistically insignificant; unclear which improvements are reliable.

Out-of-distribution evaluation incomplete: OOD experiment (§A.3) limited to one synthetic shortcut scenario (white circle). Real OOD generalization (ImageNet-v2, corrupted images, different domains) not evaluated; unclear how amortized explainer generalizes when training-test distribution shifts.

Missing ablations on key components: No quantified ablation on grid augmentation benefit, regularization λ_reg sensitivity, Sinkhorn iterations (why 30?), training epochs (why one?), or total training cost comparison. These gaps make reproducibility and design understanding difficult.

strengths: Well-motivated technical approach: Framing attribution metric optimization as differentiable permutation learning via Gumbel-Sinkhorn is intuitive and elegant
Strong empirical results: Achieves competitive or superior performance on most metrics while maintaining inference efficiency (0.016s vs. 13.6s for MDA)
Visually compelling qualitative improvements: Demonstrates notably sharper, boundary-aligned attributions compared to baselines, particularly for ViTs (Figure 1)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple architectures (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt-S), diverse metrics (Deletion, Insertion, Positive, Negative, ADP, PIC), multiple reference images, extensive ablations
Thoughtful system design: Region-based permutation, perturbation step sampling, and grid augmentation show practical engineering to scale training without overfitting to spatial artifacts
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-articulated motivation, detailed implementation specifications, code promised to be available
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Gumbel-Sinkhorn is an existing technique (Mena et al. 2018); contribution is primarily in application rather than methodological innovation, making the work somewhat incremental

Severe practical limitations undermine 'amortized' efficiency claims: Requires retraining explainer on ImageNet-1K for each new target model, severely limiting applicability to practitioners working with many models; requires representative training data, making it inaccessible for proprietary/closed-source models

Narrow evaluation scope limits generalizability: Only ImageNet-1K classification evaluated; no results on medical imaging, segmentation, or other domains; only 3 architectures tested; crucially, no human evaluation studies to validate that improved metrics translate to better user-understood explanations

Theoretical gaps in approximation quality: Method optimizes several approximations (soft masks, region-level perturbations, sampled steps S=16) but provides no analysis of approximation error or tightness; no justification for why S=16 suffices; no error propagation analysis

Test-time refinement gains raise concerns about zero-shot performance: Without refinement (T=0), improvements are often marginal; with T=3, gains are substantial but runtime increases significantly, undermining claimed efficiency advantage and raising questions about true practical utility

Substantial metric sensitivity and evaluation limitations: Metrics show large variance across reference images (Tables 5-7); Deletion/Insertion have known shortcomings (sensitivity to reference choice, perturbation strategy); no downstream task evaluation (model debugging, robustness analysis)

Incomplete hyperparameter and sensitivity analysis: Many hyperparameters (G ∈ [7,28], S=16, τ, λ_reg=2.5×10^-3, etc.) with ablations only on T and S; grid range selection appears arbitrary; no sensitivity analysis for regularization strength or temperature parameter

Architecture-specific design choices not validated: Explainer uses frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone without justification; no experiments on encoder choice sensitivity; method appears somewhat over-engineered for ViTs despite generality claims

Fair comparison concerns: Explainer trained on full ImageNet-1K with varying baseline training histories; runtime comparison with MDA conflates speed vs. quality optimization; missing simpler baselines (e.g., pixel-level explainer trained to mimic propagation-based methods)

Stability and robustness undercharacterized: Substantial performance variance between predicted and ground-truth classes suggests brittleness; no failure mode analysis; no statistical significance testing despite 50K image evaluation set; no discussion of when refinement becomes necessary

strengths: Novel application of Gumbel-Sinkhorn to create differentiable deletion/insertion metrics through soft permutation matrices; elegant insight that these metrics depend only on relative ordering
Effectively bridges three attribution paradigms (propagation-based efficiency, perturbation-based causal grounding, amortized learning), addressing documented limitations of each

Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple metrics (Deletion, Insertion, Positive/Negative, ADP, PIC), multiple architectures (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt), competitive/superior results, 10-15x runtime improvement over MDA
Produces dense, pixel-level attributions for vision transformers without patch-level upsampling artifacts; sharp, boundary-aligned results in qualitative evaluations
Well-motivated practical design choices (region-based permutation, grid augmentation, test-time refinement) with proper ablations and clear compute-quality tradeoffs

Thorough experimental documentation: detailed per-reference-image results, architecture-agnostic applicability, out-of-distribution evaluation, extensive qualitative examples, and comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Gumbel-Sinkhorn and soft permutation matrices are established techniques; contribution is primarily their application to this problem rather than fundamental innovation
Model-specific training requirement (must retrain for each target model) significantly limits practical applicability; amortization overhead and transferability across models insufficiently discussed

Proxy metric limitations under-explored: method optimizes approximations of deletion/insertion metrics (which themselves have known shortcomings); no formal analysis of soft relaxation quality or cumulative approximation error from region-level and step-sampling approximations

Training procedure complexity not fully addressed: multiple sensitive hyperparameters (G, S, τ, λ values), grid augmentation appears necessary to prevent overfitting, regularization needed for spurious peaks; less plug-and-play than propagation-based alternatives
No theoretical analysis: missing convergence guarantees for Gumbel-Sinkhorn iterations, bounds on approximation quality, and characterization of cumulative error from multiple relaxations

Incomplete analysis of metric-specific performance: variable results on Insertion metric (Tables 1-2); missing ablations isolating deletion vs. insertion objective contributions and explaining performance variations

Generalization scope limited: only ImageNet classification evaluated; applicability to other datasets, tasks (detection, segmentation), and model types unclear; domain shift addressed only via artificial shortcut experiment
Architectural transparency lacking: choice of frozen DINOv3 backbone not justified; sensitivity to backbone architecture and possibility of simpler alternatives not explored

Fairness of comparisons: MDA is per-sample adaptive while AHA is amortized (fundamentally different paradigms); 'zero-shot' outperformance claims (T=0 vs MDA) somewhat misleading; fixed-budget comparison would be more informative

Missing ablations and analyses: relative importance of different approximations (region-level vs. step-sampling vs. grid augmentation), impact of freezing backbone, sensitivity to temperature τ, and failure modes not discussed
